demonstration_summary.title: ${var.title} complete
demonstration_summary.summary: The walkthrough answered “${scenario.title}” by building the evidence in three layers instead of treating the incident report as proof. It bounded Discover to the relevant ${var.window_spelled}, used KQL to test for ${var.finding_phrase}, and then checked an individual event to confirm that finding in the context of ${truth.scope}.

checks.title: Scope
checks.detail: The global time picker was set to the last ${var.window_spelled} because the briefing reported the incident first noticed ${detected_offset_minutes} minutes ago, matching that boundary before any pattern was interpreted. Discover refreshed its histogram and result set inside that interval, removing older background history that could otherwise make the later comparison misleading.

checks.title: Signal
checks.detail: The KQL query “${var.query}” used ${var.field} to remove unrelated events and isolate records pointing to ${var.finding_phrase}. The filtered result set established that the signal exists within ${truth.scope}, while leaving the document-level inspection to test whether the match was genuinely relevant.

checks.title: Evidence
checks.detail: A representative filtered event was expanded and its individual fields were read together. That check confirmed that ${var.finding_phrase} and ${truth.scope} coexist in a real event, guarding against a conclusion based only on a histogram, count, or coincidental field value.

demonstration_summary.evidence: The KQL result set supplied the primary signal, and the expanded event supplied independent document-level corroboration. Because both evidence layers point to ${var.finding_phrase} within ${truth.scope}, they support the same interpretation rather than relying on the incident wording alone.
demonstration_summary.conclusion: ${truth.conclusion} This conclusion is supported by both the scoped, filtered result set and a representative event whose fields corroborate the same finding.

answer.evidence: The KQL result and expanded event connect ${var.finding_phrase} to ${truth.scope}.

goals.title: Set the time window
goals.concept: Setting a time range separates the incident from everyday, background activity.
goals.narration: Set the time window before you start reading the data.
goals.reasoning: A set time range keeps older, unrelated data from throwing off the comparison.
goals.evidence: The histogram and results should refresh to the window you picked.

demonstration.narration: Set the time picker at the top to the last ${var.window_spelled}. The report said this incident was first noticed ${detected_offset_minutes} minutes ago, so the last ${var.window_spelled} covers that moment and drops the older, unrelated data around it.
demonstration.reasoning: We pick the window from the one solid fact the report gave us — that the incident was noticed ${detected_offset_minutes} minutes ago — and the last ${var.window_spelled} keeps that moment in view with a bit of room on each side. That way the records for ${truth.scope} sit next to the normal traffic around them, instead of being compared against older, unrelated data, before we look for ${var.finding_phrase}.
demonstration.evidence: Once the range is set, the histogram and result count refresh to the last ${var.window_spelled}. We haven't proved a cause yet — we've just narrowed Discover to the window the report's “noticed ${detected_offset_minutes} minutes ago” points at, so the next search over ${truth.scope} actually means something.

hints: Start with when the reported problem happened.
Use the date picker at the top of Discover (or click and drag on the date histogram); for a live view you can also turn on auto-refresh.
Set the range to the last ${var.window_spelled}; Show me can do it for you.

goals.title: Isolate the decisive records
goals.concept: A query should narrow the evidence without assuming more than the brief establishes.
goals.narration: Use KQL to isolate the field pattern that answers the operational question.
goals.reasoning: Filtering the decisive field makes the abnormal group comparable with normal records.
goals.evidence: The remaining result set contains the scenario signal.

demonstration.narration: The window from the last step still contains normal, healthy traffic, so enter this KQL query in the search bar: ${var.query}. It uses ${var.field} to narrow this run to the records most likely to reveal ${var.finding_phrase}.
demonstration.reasoning: The scoped window still contains normal and background events. Filtering on ${var.field} removes that noise and tests whether evidence for ${var.finding_phrase} is actually present in ${truth.scope}, instead of assuming the brief is correct.
demonstration.evidence: When the query runs, the table should shrink to the scenario signal. Look for ${var.field} values and neighbouring fields that point to ${var.finding_phrase}; that result supports, but does not yet fully corroborate, “${truth.conclusion}”

hints: Identify the field that separates the abnormal records.

Use the KQL bar — combine clauses with and/or/not and parentheses, match with * wildcards or test a field with field:* — or Add filter (field, operator, value) and filter for or out (is not) a value from a row or a field's top values.
Filter on ${var.field}; Show me can enter a reference query.

goals.title: Check the evidence in one event
goals.concept: A conclusion is stronger when you open one typical event and check it.
goals.narration: Open one typical result and read the fields that back up the finding.
goals.reasoning: Checking a single event stops you from drawing a conclusion from totals alone.
goals.evidence: The event you open contains the facts that back up the finding.

demonstration.narration: Expand the first filtered result and read its fields one by one. We expect one real event to connect ${var.finding_phrase} with ${truth.scope}, rather than asking you to trust just the histogram or the result count.
demonstration.reasoning: A total can look convincing even when it's made up of the wrong kind of event or an unrelated record. Opening one typical event checks that the key values really do appear together in the same event and back up the filtered signal.
demonstration.evidence: The event you opened is the evidence that backs it up. If its fields match ${var.finding_phrase} and ${truth.scope}, then the signal and the event together support the conclusion: ${truth.conclusion}

hints: Check one typical record instead of relying only on the count.
Expand a row, open a field's top values, or change the table — add the key field as a column, or hide one you don't need.
Open the first result; Show me can do it for you.

goals.title: Submit a conclusion you can back up
goals.concept: A good answer states the finding, its scope, and the evidence that links them.
goals.narration: Write down the conclusion and point to the evidence for it.
goals.reasoning: The answer should keep what you saw separate from what you worked out.
goals.evidence: The answer points to the signal and the event that backs it up.
